problem: Autonomous navigation typically depends on accurate positioning (GPS/SLAM/LiDAR) and extensive sensor data or training on the target environment, which is costly and fails where signals are obstructed. Prior landmark-based methods need labeled data from the target environment.
motivation: Humans navigate with a few landmarks and concise instructions. The paper wants a robot to follow a route in an unseen environment given only one or a few images of key waypoints paired with high-level actions (e.g. turn left), making adoption in new environments cheap and independent of positioning hardware.
key_idea: Split navigation into a few-shot waypoint detector (metric learning with Gaussian distribution embeddings and a symmetrized Mahalanobis distance) that triggers high-level actions from a lookup table, and a conditional end-to-end imitation-learned maneuver controller that executes them.
insight: Distribution embeddings compared with a symmetrized Mahalanobis distance give the best offline accuracy (92.8% with self-supervised pretraining, multivariate input), and backbone pretraining matters a lot (56.4% without vs 92.8%). Self-supervised (SwAV) pretraining generally beats supervised ImageNet pretraining. The offline accuracy underestimates real performance because most false positives are early detections that are harmless online. Lowering the threshold from 0.65 to 0.5 removed all online failures. The detector is robust to occlusion and brightness change but collapses under blur and noise (49.9%), which were absent from the training augmentations.
method: Route teaching: choose waypoints where a new action is needed, assign a discrete action to each in a lookup table (LUT), and store one or a few example images per waypoint as memory prototypes (no fine-tuning on the new route).

Distribution embedding: ResNet-50 backbone (SwAV self-supervised ImageNet init) followed by a linear mean head and a 2-layer fully connected covariance head with Softplus for diagonal variance. Per-frame distributions from s=10 consecutive frames are combined by averaging means and covariances.

Symmetrized Mahalanobis distance: distance between the query distribution and the class distribution using the averaged covariance (Σ_q+Σ_class)/2. A 4-layer classifier with sigmoid outputs the probability that the waypoint is reached, trained with BCE on episodic tasks (1 positive and 6 negative queries).

Two-phase training: phase 1 freezes the backbone and trains the mean, covariance and classifier heads; phase 2 fine-tunes everything. Episodes are sampled from laps of different courses, with positives taken near the turn.

Inference: 6 sliding-window memory distributions per waypoint from a single lap, the max match probability is compared to a threshold (0.65 from validation, 0.5 default), and the detected waypoint's action is looked up.

Conditional maneuver controller: EfficientNet-B0 features from two fisheye cameras are concatenated with a one-hot action (left/right/straight) and passed to an MLP that outputs steering (throttle fixed). Trained with MSE by imitation, with flip augmentation that mirrors steering and action. The last action is held until the next waypoint is detected.

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (SwAV-pretrained, fine-tuned) for waypoint detection + EfficientNet-B0 for steering control
setting.training_data: Own dataset of 36 indoor courses in 11 UC Davis buildings (2-8 laps each); 12 CW/CCW pairs for training, 6 courses for validation, the rest for testing. Controller trained on the test locations too, with repeated runs and random actions at intersections. Backbone initialised from self-supervised ImageNet.
setting.observation: Two 180° fisheye RGB cameras (60° apart), resized to 224x224 per camera
setting.action_space: High-level discrete actions (left/right/straight) from a LUT plus a continuous steering output with fixed throttle
setting.privileged: Example images of each waypoint from a prior lap (memory lap) plus the ordered waypoint list and actions; the controller was trained on the test locations; manual reset of the waypoint ID after failure

numbers_note: No standard benchmark; results are on the authors' own indoor dataset (offline waypoint detection accuracy and online real-car course/waypoint success).
results: Offline waypoint-detection accuracy on 6 unseen courses reaches 92.8% with self-supervised pretraining and the symmetrized Mahalanobis distance, above Euclidean at 89.4% in the same configuration. Online on a real car, threshold 0.65 gave 23/28 course-level and 266/272 waypoint-level successes. Threshold 0.5 gave 7/7 courses and 68/68 waypoints in a limited test.
limitations: Small proof of concept: indoor corridors of a single campus, small RC car, only 3 actions, throttle fixed, and the controller was trained on the test locations.
A missed or false waypoint detection throws the vehicle off-path with no recovery, and the ordered waypoint list is assumed; the 0.5 threshold was tested only once per route.
Very fragile to image-quality corruptions (blur and noise drop accuracy to 49.9%), and offline accuracy is a proxy for real performance.
compares_to: supervised vs self-supervised vs no backbone pretraining
